hints.title: Evaluate the integral first
hints.body: Treat n as a constant and integrate with respect to x.
hints.recap: An integral can contain a constant parameter as well as its integration variable.
hints.pitfall: The factor outside the integral applies to the entire result.
hints.pause: Apply both limits, then divide the result by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math> to find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>.

recall.reminder: An integral can contain a constant parameter as well as its integration variable.

hints.title: Write out the first few summands
hints.body: Use your formula to write F(1), F(2) and F(3). Identify the sequence and sum its first n terms.
hints.recap: Writing a few terms can reveal the pattern hidden by sigma notation.
hints.pitfall: In the sum, replace the input of F by r.

recall.reminder: Writing a few terms can reveal the pattern hidden by sigma notation.

hints.title: Check the integer boundary
hints.body: Use your formula to locate where G(n) passes 150. Check the neighbouring whole numbers.
hints.pitfall: Finding an integer that works is not enough: the previous one must fail.
hints.pause: Show which smallest positive integer meets the strict inequality.

solution:
The straight-line sketch provides a check: the integral equals the triangular area, before the external normalising factor is applied.

F(n)=(1n)[nx−x22]0n =n2. Therefore G(n)= ∑r = 1nr2 =n(n+1)4.

The inequality is n(n+1)>600. At n=24, the product is exactly 600 and the strict inequality fails. At n=25 it is 650 and succeeds. The product is increasing for positive integers, so this is the least possible n.

Answer D: 25.
